title: Carbon Dating: Reading Time in Atoms
hook: Every living thing is a slowly ticking clock. The moment it dies, a radioactive form of carbon starts running down — and counting what's left tells us how long ago that was.
key_points: Living things absorb a steady trace of radioactive carbon-14 along with ordinary carbon.
At death, intake stops and the carbon-14 decays with a half-life of about 5,730 years.
Measuring how much carbon-14 remains reveals time since death.
It works back to roughly 50,000 years — great for remains, not for dinosaurs or rocks.
content_html: Carbon dating turns radioactive decay into a calendar. The atmosphere holds a tiny, fairly steady fraction of carbon-14, a radioactive form of carbon, mixed in with ordinary carbon. Living things constantly exchange carbon with their surroundings — by eating, breathing, photosynthesizing — so while alive they carry that same small fraction of carbon-14. The clock isn't running yet, because whatever decays is continuously topped up.
extra_html: Death stops the resupply. From that moment, the carbon-14 already in the body simply decays away, with a half-life of about 5,730 years, while the stable carbon stays put. So if a bone or piece of charcoal has only half the expected carbon-14, it's been roughly one half-life — about 5,730 years — since the organism died; a quarter means two half-lives, and so on. This makes carbon dating a workhorse of archaeology, pinning ages of wood, cloth, bone, and ash. Its reach is limited: after about 50,000 years so little carbon-14 remains that it can't be measured reliably, so dinosaurs and old rocks are dated instead with longer-lived isotopes like uranium. Wikipedia explains the method and its calibration.

related.title: Radioactivity and Half-Life
related.hook: You can't predict when a single unstable atom will decay, yet a huge sample decays on a clock so precise we use it to date rocks billions of years old.

related.title: Inside the Atom
related.hook: An atom is almost entirely empty space wrapped around a tiny, dense nucleus — and the number of protons in that nucleus is what makes an atom gold instead of oxygen.

flashcards.prompt: What starts the 'clock' that carbon dating reads?
flashcards.back_html: Death. While alive, a thing keeps replenishing its carbon-14; once it dies, intake stops and the carbon-14 only decays from then on.

flashcards.prompt: How does measuring leftover carbon-14 tell you an object's age?

choices.text: Carbon-14 decays at a known half-life, so the amount left maps to elapsed time
Older objects simply contain more carbon-14
Carbon-14 changes color as it ages

flashcards.explanation_html: With a half-life near 5,730 years, half is gone after one half-life, three-quarters after two, and so on — so the fraction remaining pins down the time since death.

flashcards.prompt: Why can't carbon dating be used to date dinosaur fossils or ancient rocks?

choices.text: After tens of thousands of years, too little carbon-14 is left to measure
Carbon-14 only decays inside living bodies

flashcards.explanation_html: Beyond about 50,000 years almost all the carbon-14 has decayed. Far older samples are dated with isotopes that have much longer half-lives.
